text: Johnson does not found his judgment upon his own admiration; the admiration of a single critic may be no more than the taste of one age and the bent of one temper. He asks what time has done to the work. The writer whose reputation rests on the fashion of his day, on the customs of a place or the quarrels of a party, may be applauded while that fashion continues; but fashions decay, and the applause that hung upon them decays as well. Only those works can be said to have proved their worth which go on pleasing readers who share none of the circumstances of the first audience, since such readers come to the trial without partiality. They were never the author's friends, they have no stake in his opinions, and they read him for no reason but that he still gives pleasure.
